analysis.one_liner: Ends a list of oil company tax breaks and uses the money to send a gas price rebate to taxpayers.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal oil company tax breaks and pay households a $500 gas price rebate died in the House Ways and Means Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal a list of tax breaks that lower the tax bills of oil and gas companies — including credits for marginal wells and enhanced oil recovery, the deduction for intangible drilling costs, percentage depletion, and special accounting rules for the biggest oil companies. It would use the revenue to send every eligible taxpayer a one-time rebate for 2022: $500 per person ($1,000 per couple) plus $500 for each dependent age 16 or older, refundable so people who owe little or no income tax get it too. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers get a refundable 2022 gas prices rebate: $500 per individual ($1,000 per joint return) plus $500 for each dependent age 16 or older, paid even to people who owe no income tax [S2][S3]. Households hurt by high gas prices in 2022 gain directly. Anyone who wants tax dollars no longer flowing to profitable oil companies as tax breaks also benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary taxpayers who paid high 2022 gas prices

how_it_helps.text: Sends every eligible taxpayer a refundable 2022 gas prices rebate of $500 ($1,000 for joint returns) plus $500 for each dependent age 16 or older, paid regardless of income tax owed

Funds the rebate by repealing tax breaks that reduce what oil companies pay: credits for marginal wells and enhanced oil recovery, the intangible drilling cost deduction, percentage depletion, the tertiary injectants deduction, and the passive loss exception for oil and gas working interests

Denies the qualified business income deduction to oil and gas activities and bars major integrated oil companies from using last-in, first-out accounting, which can defer taxes by inflating the cost of inventory
Limits the foreign tax credit for oil companies that pay levies to foreign governments in exchange for specific economic benefits, so those payments count less as a credit against U.S. tax
Expands the crude oil excise tax to cover oil from tar sands and oil shale, extending the tax that finances oil spill liability funds to those fuels

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies, especially large integrated producers, pay through the loss of tax credits, deductions, favorable accounting methods, and foreign tax credit rules; the expanded excise tax would also fall on tar sands and oil shale producers, whose costs could be passed to consumers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies losing tax breaks

drawbacks.text: The rebate is retroactive — it compensates for 2022 gas prices in a bill introduced in March 2023 — so it provides no relief going forward and would simply add to federal borrowing when paid

Repealing the enhanced oil recovery credit also ends a credit used for carbon dioxide injection projects, which some climate policy supporters rely on; the bill eliminates the credit outright rather than reforming it
Industry and some economists argue that raising oil companies' tax costs gets passed through to consumers at the pump, meaning drivers could pay at the gas station what they receive back as a rebate
The bill never drew Republican support and only three cosponsors, leaving no evidence of the coalition needed to move tax legislation through a committee controlled by the other party

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: the bill shifts tax burden from households to oil companies and pays families a rebate for a year of high gas prices. Its biggest design flaw is timing — a 2022 rebate introduced in 2023 is backward-looking cash, not future protection. Repealing the enhanced oil recovery credit also sweeps away a tool some carbon capture projects depend on. Those flaws are arguments for a better version, not for keeping the tax breaks; the bill's failure means ordinary households got no rebate and oil companies kept every preference it targeted.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or any vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 23, 2023 and referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
No hearing, markup, vote, or further action of any kind followed; the complete action history ends with the referral
The bill attracted only its sponsor and three Democratic cosponsors and never moved in the Republican-controlled committee
When the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, the bill expired without a vote

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies are better off: they kept the tax credits, deductions, and accounting preferences the bill would have repealed, and no offsetting rebate reached taxpayers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies that kept tax breaks

for.name: Rep. Sean Casten
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its case for repealing oil company tax breaks to fund consumer rebates

for.name: Reps. Blumenauer, Levin, and McClellan
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only support it attracted

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote; it sat in committee from referral until the Congress ended

against.name: Fossil fuel industry lobbying
against.what_they_did: Fought past efforts to repeal oil and gas tax preferences, which remain law; its interest ran against this bill

sides.party_line_note: All four original sponsors and all three cosponsors were Democrats; the bill received no Republican support and the Republican-led Ways and Means Committee took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would repeal a long list of oil and gas tax preferences: the marginal well and enhanced oil recovery credits, the intangible drilling cost deduction, percentage depletion, the tertiary injectants deduction, and the passive loss exception for working interests. Keeping these breaks keeps money flowing to the industry that would otherwise fund the rebate.

The bill bars major integrated oil companies from LIFO accounting and denies them the qualified business income deduction and broader foreign tax credit benefits. These companies are large enough that the accounting change alone carries a meaningful tax bill.

industries.industry: Tar sands and oil shale producers
industries.note: The bill expands the definition of crude oil for the petroleum excise tax to include tar sands and oil shale-derived oil, subjecting those producers to the tax that funds oil spill cleanup trust funds.

industries.industry: Carbon capture and CO2 injection services
industries.note: The bill repeals the credit for enhanced oil recovery, which some operators use for carbon dioxide injection projects marketed as carbon capture. Environmental groups split on this credit because it can subsidize more oil production even when it also stores carbon.
